A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LLM-as-a-judge validation framework despite the changed title and substantial reorganization. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original synthetic experiments and evaluations of five LLM judges on Civil Comments toxicity ratings, including decision consistency, prevalence bias and sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: V3 reports original evaluations involving eight LLM judges and eleven rating tasks, alongside synthetic experiments and analyses using reconstructed human response-set distributions.

M1.justification: V1 already contains response-set elicitation, the reverse rating model and multi-label MSE. V3 adds an estimated-transition variant that uses an auxiliary corpus of paired forced-choice and response-set ratings to estimate shared conditional probabilities before reconstructing human multi-label vectors (Section 3.4; Appendix D). This is a limited procedural extension of the existing framework.

E1.justification: V1's real-data evaluation covers Civil Comments toxicity. V3 retains it and adds SNLI, MNLI, AlphaNLI, QAGS, four SummEval dimensions and two TopicalChat dimensions (Table 3). Coverage substantially expands into natural-language and abductive inference, summarization quality and factuality, and dialogue evaluation.

E2.justification: Most comparator metrics already appear in v1, including both KL-divergence and cross-entropy directions, JSD, Cohen's kappa, Fleiss's kappa and Coverage. V3 adds Krippendorff's alpha to the real-data comparisons (Figure 9), whereas v1 reports it in synthetic experiments but omits it from its real-data Tables 3–4. This is a limited comparator-set expansion.

E3.justification: V3 introduces oracle-versus-estimated-transition evaluation and aggregates downstream selection regret across tasks and threshold sweeps. The candidate pool adds Claude 3 Haiku, DeepSeek Chat and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and new SummEval experiments binarize ratings at 4 on the original 1–5 scale. Civil Comments sampling is also reported differently: v1 uses 10–50% toxicity-annotation strata, while v3 specifies an agreement range of 0.2–0.5.

E4.justification: V3 adds an oracle-versus-estimated-transition analysis (Figure 4), task/model sensitivity-parameter analyses (Figures 5 and 10), and a synthetic case study of categorical-score saturation and tied selections (Figure 35). Core rater-error robustness analyses remain in Figures 36–38. V1's standalone human-only finite-sample analyses in Figure 6, left, and Figure 15 are omitted.

E5.justification: V3 adds error bars to real-data performance comparisons and boxplots of sensitivity estimates (Figures 4–6 and 10), whereas v1's real-data case study reports point estimates. V1 already includes uncertainty bands in synthetic experiments. The construction of these displays and seed counts remain unspecified, so additional reporting does not establish increased replication.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive taskwise rankings and oracle/estimated-MSE results (Figures 4, 6 and 11–21). For example, Section 4.2 and Figure 6 report an additional 0.28 fluency-prevalence bias when GPT-3.5 Turbo is selected using KL(j,h), compared with selecting Claude Sonnet 3.5 by downstream bias. These substantially extend v1's five-judge toxicity results; changed sampling and candidate pools prevent a controlled same-setting performance comparison.

T1.justification: The decomposition, identifiability and rank-consistency theorems, rater-error lemma, proofs and worked counterexamples are retained in v3 Appendices C and F. A limited definitional revision replaces v1 Definition 2.1's underspecified criterion, |O| <= |Q|, with v3 Section 3.3 explicitly treating equality as fully specified, removing the earlier equality-case ambiguity.

C1.justification: The central warning that forced-choice validation can misrank judges under indeterminacy remains unchanged. V3 adds the specific contribution that useful response-set MSE validation can be recovered using a small paired auxiliary corpus and makes this a main recommendation. The abstract's headline performance deficit changes from 34% to 30% under the revised experiments.

C2.justification: V3 favors response-set MSE and recommends KL(h,j) as a forced-choice fallback, replacing v1's practical JSD recommendation. It adds substantive explanations involving evaluator-controlled ambiguity resolution and categorical-score saturation, plus limitations concerning discrete scales, rater homogeneity, cognitive burden and resource tradeoffs (Section 5; Appendices E/G). V1's specific criticism of prediction-powered inference is removed.

D1.justification: V3 newly documents temperature 1.0, ten LLM draws per item, invalid-response handling, prompts for all eleven tasks, and supplementary-code reproduction instructions (Section 4.1; Appendices A/D). These substantially expand v1's limited real-experiment documentation. Reproduction remains partly ambiguous: Section 4.2 specifies 100 auxiliary paired ratings, while Appendix D specifies 200; referenced code availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

R1.justification: V3 adds substantial related-work discussions in Section 2 and Appendix B, positioning the framework against Elangovan et al.'s distributional alternative and connecting it to perspectivist NLP/HCI, perceptual psychology and rating-process models. Numerous substantive citations accompany this expanded positioning. The earlier prediction-powered-inference discussion and associated references are removed.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the introduction and framework narrative, adds dedicated related-work and practical-limitations sections, and centers the main experiments on multiple real rating tasks. Much of v1's detailed theoretical development and synthetic study moves into appendices, with a new notation guide. This substantially changes exposition and organization beyond the title change.

P2.justification: The document changes from two-column to single-column presentation and substantially redesigns its visual explanation. V3 adds a motivating ranking figure, a matrix-based rating-model illustration, an aggregation summary table, aggregate regret plots, taskwise ranking plots and additional prompt panels. Earlier synthetic figures are regrouped or relocated, and the toxicity results are reorganized from numerical tables into graphical comparisons.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens the empirical support beyond v1's single toxicity case and tests whether estimated transitions can approximate oracle-MSE selections. Clearer exposition, expanded implementation instructions and explicit applicability limits improve usability and assessability. Human response-set truth remains assumption-dependent, and the 100-versus-200 auxiliary-sample discrepancy and Figure 9's reversed KL-direction guidance weaken reproducibility. These localized problems do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and practical guidance.
